While GPUs have powered the AI boom and are widely used to accelerate HPC workloads, they’re not the best fit for every computing challenge. Sparse workloads, in particular, represent a big mismatch with GPU capabilities. That’s one reason why the Jülich Supercomputing Center (JSC) today announced that it has tapped Sparxity (formerly SpiNNcloud) to provide neuromorphic systems to accelerate sparse machine learning workloads.
Sparxity is a spinoff from a neuromorphic computing research project that spanned the University of Dresden and University of Manchester. The company, which was founded as SpiNNcloud in 2021, originally sought to build a neuromorphic chip for accelerating spiking neural network (SNNs).
JUBIS installed at JSC (Image courtesy Sparxity)
Over time, the company focused its efforts on accelerating a broader range of sparse computing workloads. According to Sparxity CEO and Founder Hector Gonzalez, that encompasses two main areas, including sparse machine learning workloads that are common in the traditional HPC community as well as accelerating the AI inference involving mixture of experts (MoE) models.
The company has developed a neuromorphic chip, dubbed the SpiNNaker2, which includes 152 processing cores. Each computing board contains 48 chips, or 7,296 cores per board. The JUBIS system being deployed at JSC contains 90 boards across several racks, representing 656,640 SpiNNaker2 cores in the multi-million-dollar deployment.
The JUBIS system will be installed in proximity to the Jupiter Booster, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer, and it’s designed to take over and run sparse machine learning workloads, such as sparse solvers and sparse optimizers, that won’t be good match to the Jupiter Booster or other JSC systems.
“Sparse machine learning represents one of the biggest opportunities to fundamentally improve the efficiency of AI,” said Dr. Guido Trensch of the Simulation and Data Lab Neuroscience at JSC. “By adopting Sparxity, we’re able to complement our globally unique HPC infrastructure with a fundamentally new approach, opening up new research opportunities so that we can further develop advancements in neuroscience.”
Sparxity developed its chip and its systems specifically to maximize computing efficiency for sparse workloads, Gonzalaz said.
Spinnaker2 boards (Image courtesy Sparxity)
“Essentially we have our systems architecture to enable event-based communication and computation,” he told HPCwire in an interview this week. “You have many, many low power cores that are highly interconnected inside every chip that we have. You have like a network on chip that basically allows you to connect chips to chips, and it allows you to scale like a very large-scale toroidal network, where you have many low power cores that talk to each other in real time and also exchange information in a very event-based or energy proportional approach.”
GPUs were designed to excel at dense workloads, where the matrices or tensors have relatively few elements with a value of zero. This is comparable to an image where most of the pixels contain some color, as opposed to being blank or dark. When the data is sparse–that is, when the image has a lot of blank or dark pixels–the GPU does not process the data faster. Instead of chugging through dense matrix-matrix multiplication, which the GPU is good at, the processor is asked to essentially process much skinnier scalars.
HPC experts Jack Dongarra, Satoshi Matsuoaka, and Torsten Hoefler touched on this earlier this year in their paper “Do We Still Need GPUs? Rethinking AI and Scientific Computing on Matrix-Enhanced CPUs .”
“Scientific computing is broader than dense matrix multiplication,” Dongarra, Matsuoka, and Hoefler wrote. “Many important applications involve sparse matrices, graph-like data structures, adaptive meshes, particles, multiscale coupling, irregular memory access, global reductions, and communication across distributed systems.”
This is the same challenge that Gonzales and Sparxity are tackling with its Spinnaker2 chip and systems. In addition to providing a much more efficient way to process sparse machine learning workloads, such as finite element analysis, the chips also excel at running some of the newer AI models.
MOE models are increasingly sparse (Image courtesy Sparxity)
When the AI boom first took off, the LLMs were designed to take advantage of GPU’s sweet spot, which was dense matrix-matrix multiplication. AI models with hundreds of billions and then trillions of activated parameters represented a dense workload that was a good match to GPUs.
But as the AI boom wore on, the community introduced mixture of experts (MOE) models. Instead of one humongous LLM with all of its parameters activated, MOEs have a combination of smaller LLMs, and only the parameters that are needed to answer a given problem are activated. So instead of dense workloads, the workload became much sparser, which is one of the reasons why GPUs are in less demand for AI inference and why CPUs are in demand (although there are other reasons, such as CPUs being better at the general compute needed for inference, KV cache calculations, tool calling, etc.)
The MOE trend has continued, and today many of the top foundation models from the US and China are becoming sparser. However, that’s creating a mismatch with the largely GPU-based systems that AI has so far relied on, Gonzalez says.
“There are a bunch of scaling laws that actually dictate the desire of going to this extreme level of sparsity,” Gonzalez said. “The more you increase the number of experts that are very small, the more you jump into these different performance curves, which are very attractive at larger parameter counts, because essentially you are getting into very intelligent models that have strong expressivity characteristics.
In addition to sparsity, another factor is granularity, which refers to how small the expert is. With a larger number of experts, the size of each expert gets smaller (assuming the same size LLM). The next generation of Sparxity’s hardware will focus more on optimizing computing for granularity, Gonzalez said.
“We basically are positioning ourselves in a very complementary angle, basically designing systems that are good at dealing with the sparse workloads,” he said. “We have already this strong traction into HPC workloads, and we are actually leaning a bit more into the mainstream space.”
Sparxity today has dozens of deployed systems at 30 customers around the world, Gonzalez said. Sandia National Laboratories is one of its HPC customers in the U.S.
The CEO also commented on the new name for the company. “Behind the new name is first showing the commitment around sparse workloads,” he said. “It’s also tying our roots on the neuromorphic side of things without actually bringing alongside the association with neuromorphic computing things, but rather more positioning into the strategic commitment that the company is doing. As I mentioned, like the our commitment is around sparse workloads.

Toto Finance Founder and Chairman Monty Metzger (L) chats with TNM’s Western Editor, Henry Lazenby, late last month at the Mining Forum Americas in Colorado Springs.
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 28, 2026
Toto Finance aims to help miners raise money by selling digital claims on copper before it leaves the ground, founder and chairman Monty Metzger told The Northern Miner in Colorado Springs.
Metzger outlines that vision in his new book, Tokenization: Capital for Humanity . His U.S.-based company is developing digital claims on refined copper stored in Arizona and on future mine production. Its first warehouse-backed copper transaction was still in the making when he spoke late last month at the Mining Forum Americas.
“They don’t like to wait 30 days for a settlement of a trade,” Metzger said of technology investors funding industrial projects. “They don’t want paper trails and DocuSigns and sending around.”
For miners, the pitch is access to capital ahead of production; for buyers building data centres and other infrastructure, it’s a way to secure future supply. Toto now must show it can raise money for miners before production starts and ensure buyers get their copper on time.

Wheaton Precious Metals President and CEO Haytham Hodaly in conversation with TNM’s Western Editor, Henry Lazenby, late last month at the Mining Forum Americas in Colorado Springs.
Posted By: Henry Lazenby October 28, 2026
Wheaton Precious Metals (TSX, NYSE, LSE: WPM) expects to repay its debt and have $4 billion (C$5.6 billion) available for new deals by the end of next year, President and CEO Haytham Hodaly said.
The company is generating more than $250 million a month in free cash flow, enough to clear its $1.9 billion in net debt while rebuilding its capacity to invest, Hodaly told The Northern Miner last month in Colorado Springs. That $4 billion would include money Wheaton could borrow through its credit lines, he said.
“It’s a time in the market right now where we’re seeing more opportunities than we’ve ever seen,” Hodaly said, pointing to higher commodity prices. “So those increasing prices provide a mechanism for people to unlock value in their existing portfolios.”
Large copper projects in Latin America could provide the next opening, although Hodaly ruled out buying copper streams. Wheaton offers miners upfront funding in exchange for future deliveries of their gold and silver byproducts, giving it exposure to precious metals without having to operate the mines.

The 2027 Stratus 231VRK Travel Trailer Feels Like Home With King Bed, Coffee Bar, and Fireplace
22 photos
Photo: Bourbon RV/ That RV Girl
Couples looking for a travel trailer that feels like a small home have plenty of options to choose from, but few models deliver the same level of comfort, utility, and style as the 2027 Venture RV Stratus 231VRK.
This brand-new couple’s travel trailer is grabbing a lot of attention from the RV community, and for good reason. Venture RV outdid itself with this new floor plan, bringing together a spacious interior, modern styling, and residential comfort in a manageable size. A redesigned exterior, a king-size bed, an electric fireplace, and a dedicated coffee bar are just a few of the features that make this RV a head-turner.
Before moving further with this new model’s strengths, it’s worth mentioning a few words about the manufacturer. Located in Shipshewana, Indiana, Venture RV is a division of KZ RV, Inc., which operates as a subsidiary of Thor Industries. It has been around since 2012 and specializes in lightweight and ultra-lightweight travel trailers and fifth wheels.
Introduced in June 2026 as part of Venture RV’s Stratus Ultra-Lite lineup, the 231VRK is a dual-axle travel trailer with a large slide-out and is aimed at couples who want to spend more time on the road without giving up the comforts of home .
Photo: Bourbon RV/ That RV Girl It measures 27 feet long (8.2 meters) and 8 feet (2.4 meters) wide and is built on a robust steel frame with an advanced wood-free composite wall system (Azdel panels) and high-gloss Lamilux fiberglass on the outside. The exterior has been refreshed with new graphics and colors, complemented by a painted front cap with a windshield, giving it a sleeker, more contemporary look.
Practical features are spread around the exterior, each included with a purpose. At the front, there are two 20-pound propane tanks under an easy-access cover, along with space for a suitable battery setup. A large pass-through storage compartment provides ample space for tools, camping equipment, and other items, while a large powered patio awning with an integrated LED light strip creates a nice shaded area at camp.
Photo: Bourbon RV/ That RV Girl At the rear, the travel trailer has a bumper-mounted spare tire, a factory-installed ladder, and backup lights, and other handy features include the utility docking station, shore power connection, standard outlet, and prewiring for an observation camera. The trailer also comes with a walkable roof, four electric stabilizer jacks, and blue ground-effect underlighting that adds another modern touch.
The interior layout is designed to comfortably accommodate a couple and boasts a central living room flanked by a front bedroom and a rear kitchen. The sole slide-out expands the living area, creating a more roomy interior that fits residential-style furniture.
Finished in Warm Linen, the interior is modern and inviting. It features antique-white kitchen cabinets, wood-toned flooring, sleek upholstery, and a board-and-batten accent wall in the kitchen area. Large windows are placed in strategic spots to bring natural light into the living space, while blackout roller shades provide privacy when desired.
Photo: Bourbon RV/ That RV Girl The front bedroom is only separated from the main living area through a curtain. It offers campers a walk-around king-size bed with a premium memory-foam mattress and nightstands, wardrobes, and power outlets/charging ports on either side. Overhead cupboards and an underbed storage compartment add more room for personal belongings.
The living room’s theater seating is located in the slide-out, along with part of the kitchen, while a cleverly designed entertainment center sits near the entrance. At first sight, it may look just like a regular entertainment center with a 40-inch wall-mounted TV and a fireplace, but a closer look reveals a permanent counter space, a pull-out dual-leaf table, and storage space behind the fireplace for chairs.
It’s such an ingenious solution for a compact space , providing a generous dining table without taking up permanent floor space. When not used for dining, it can also be set up as a place to work on the laptop.
Photo: Bourbon RV/ That RV Girl The kitchen is quite wide and comfortable to work in. The cooking equipment is on the side, while the rear section is for meal prep. It integrates a large, single-bowl stainless-steel sink that comes with a cover, an integrated dish-drying rack, and a high-rise faucet with a sprayer. Appliances include an InVision oven and three-burner cooktop with a flush glass cover, a microwave, and a large refrigerator with freezer compartment. A floor-to-ceiling pantry with adjustable shelves is also included.
Another nifty addition is a dedicated coffee bar with space for your coffee machine and a bank of drawers for your barista accessories.
The bathroom shares the width of the trailer with the kitchen, which means it’s not very large. However, the space is efficiently utilized to include a full-size shower with ample headroom and shelves for toiletries, a vanity with storage underneath, a mirrored medicine cabinet, and a foot-flush porcelain toilet.
Photo: Bourbon RV/ That RV Girl Other standard features include a large wardrobe at the entrance with shoe storage and a coat rack, a designated pet-dish location, and a Safe-Tek hidden storage compartment for valuables. For climate control, the travel trailer is equipped with a Coleman Whisper air-conditioner, a 20,000 BTU ducted propane furnace, and an RV Airflow System, while the water system includes a 45-gallon fresh water tank, a 38-pound gray tank, and a 38-pound black water tank.
The RV’s listed dry weight is 5,790 pounds (2,626 kg), offering easy towability. As for pricing, it will depend on the optional packages you chose to equip it with and the dealership , but the MSPR ranges from $60,800 to $63,145.

Strong financial numbers released between Tuesday and Wednesday by C.H. Robinson and Landstar were overshadowed on Wall Street by concern over one particular issue: insurance.
Landstar kicked off the issue Tuesday afternoon with its third quarter earnings release that showed heavier than usual insurance charges.
The C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW) 3Q earnings, while not being as specific as the Landstar (NASDAQ: LSTR) report on the individual hits that drove up its insurance costs, did provide data that showed its insurance costs were abnormally high during the quarter.
Coming in a six-month period in which the broader long-term risk of insurance costs rising was driven home by expanded broker liability exposure due to Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II , and a whopping nuclear verdict that hit C.H. Robinson in Lipe vs. Lupus Superior and its subsequent affirmation by a Dallas County judge , the insurance aspects of otherwise solid earnings appeared to lead investors to effectively nullify otherwise strong financial reports.
One other negative factor cited by analysts for the slide at C.H. Robinson: operating cash flow fell to $124.1 million compared to $275.4 million a year ago. But that was sequentially an improvement from the second quarter figure of $35.9 million. The third quarter figure was said by C.H. Robinson to have been caused by “unfavorable changes in working capital driven by higher transportation rates.”
The transportation research team at Deutsche Bank cited several factors for the stock slide at C.H. Robinson, including its North American Surface Transportation gross margin compared to its peers within truckload carriers.
The numbers at the end of the day
For the day, C.H. Robinson stock was down 11.14% or $15.99 to $127.60. It marked a continuation of a slide that saw the price reach $210.33 on July 22 and was as high as $158.35 at the start of October
For Landstar, its stock closed down 17.76% or $29.98 to $138.80. Its 52-week high was $228.46 on June 8.
On the C.H. Robinson earnings call with analysts, several on the call asked a significant number of questions about the issue of insurance claims. It was a sign of a selloff that occurred despite a quarterly report that on its surface probably should have been at least neutral to the price.
What may have spooked C.H. Robinson investors was the company’s disclosure in its earnings report that its Selling, General & Administrative (SG&A) expenses were up 29.7% from a year earlier, “primarily due to higher claims expenses.” Insurance costs at C.H. Robinson are in the SG&A category.
CFO Damon Lee said SG&A for the year is expected to be $585 to $590 million compared to an earlier estimate of $540 to $580 million. While that is not all insurance–Lee said depreciation and amortization will push that figure up as well–the comment appeared to have caught analysts off guard compared to their own estimates of C.H. Robinson’s insurance costs.
Adding to that, CEO Dave Bozeman said in his introductory remarks on the earnings call that C.H. Robinson is “progressing nicely” through the 2027 insurance renewal process, “and we believe this renewal will result in insurance inflation that is reasonable and manageable.”
But Bozeman added to that an example of inflation that may have been interpreted by the analysts as signaling a higher inflation rate for insurance costs than they anticipated.
“As a reference, we’ve been absorbing approximately $30 million of annual wage inflation, and we’ve still delivered double-digit earnings growth in 2024 through 2026,” Bozeman said.
Can you clarify that?
That led UBS analyst Tom Wadewitz of UBS to ask Lee for a “clarification.”
“You said that $30 million of inflation and compensation and benefits you absorb every year, are you trying to imply like we should assume that the increase in insurance would be less than that $30 million or that magnitude?” Wadewitz said. “It seemed like you might be implying that with the way you presented that comment.”
Lee said the $30 million comparison by Bozeman and himself was “provided..as an example of magnitude, just so you guys can get your head around the headwinds that we absorb every day and never talk about.”
“We’re built to offset headwinds, we’re built to absorb inflation and still deliver demonstrable results,” Lee said. “So we thought that was a pertinent example to give, just to give you some context around how our inflation on insurance is not going to be something that derails our earnings trajectory going forward.”
Not a big deal
Lee, at another point in the call, repeated that insurance increases were not a significant threat to C.H. Robinson’s basic finances.
Lee said C.H. Robinson usually benchmarks its total insurance and claims expenses as 50 basis points of its total gross revenue. Year to date, he said, C.H. Robinson is below that number, even though third quarter numbers were relatively elevated.
Lee in a post-analysts call interview with FreightWaves, said insurance expenses as measured against gross revenue are “de minimis.”
“While our claims expenses are typically linear throughout our year, periodically, some quarters are higher than others, as demonstrated in Q3,” Lee said on the analysts’ call. “We typically look at these types of expenses on a longer trajectory than certainly one quarter, and we’re still well within that guidance.”
Hearing about it by the end of the year…possibly
Bozeman added that the insurance renewal process will be completed by the end of December, “and we will share an update on our 2027 insurance costs as soon as we can.”
The disclosure on the level of insurance increases in 2027, which are now likely to be anticipated to an almost manic degree, will likely come in mid-to-late December, Bozeman said. That is generally the time “when we get finality on what the insurance police will look like.”
He added that this year, the company is trying to get those nailed down sooner rather than later. Bozeman added he hoped the information would be available before the company’s next earnings call.
But he reiterated that insurance costs are not going to be a headwind for C.H. Robinson.
“We still feel very good about those proceedings,” Bozeman said of the insurance negotiations “We’ve said multiple times that we feel like the outcome will be close to industry leading, if not industry leading, and we certainly don’t feel like the inflation on those those costs will be anything that will derail earnings going forward.”
Bozeman reiterated a point he has made separately: “We continue to manage our legal docket as we have for years, with most cases being either dismissed or settled for amounts below our deductible.”
Issues at Landstar
On the Landstar call with analysts, CFO Jim Todd said “claim cost severity has been going up at a decent clip that we felt like for a period of years that (reserves) were sufficient.”
However, the category of incurred but not reported reserves were up 27% in terms of gross dollars from the fourth quarter of 2022 to the fourth quarter of 2025 at Landstar, Todd said, “and that’s on a declining truck count.”
Todd spelled out several metrics that showed how much Landstar’s insurance costs have risen. “We want to continue to book those higher loss estimates prospectively,” he said.
He did say two claims in the second quarter were in federal jurisdictions where there previously had been protection for brokers under the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act that was eliminated as a protection for brokers by the decision in Montgomery vs. Caribe Transport II.
Todd was asked about future estimates going forward but he demurred. “This is a highly complex environment to estimate insurance and claim reserves,” he said, adding that previous guidance on the percentage of revenues from the company’s business capacity owners (BCOs) that should go for claim reserves will no longer be disclosed.
RXO’s docket
Although the call was the first since the C.H. Robinson acquisition of RXO was announced, that subject took up relatively little time with analysts.
However, given the insurance and legal backdrop of the third quarter earnings, one aspect of the acquisition did come up: the legal landscape faced by RXO.
Bozeman reiterated a point made when the deal was announced that “RXO’s legal docket is a neutral factor when compared to our own docket. And like us, RXO has a significant insurance tower for contingent auto liability claims.

BMW's M2 Grows Muscles in All the Right Places, Albeit Only Digitally
10 photos
Photo: Instagram | rotislav_prokop
While its larger sibling, the BMW 3 Series , has already tapped into the Neue Klasse era, with the range-topping M3 joining it perhaps a few months to roughly one year from now, the 2 Series Coupe will live on for a few more years in its current form.
The second-generation entered production at San Luis Potosi in Mexico in the second half of 2021, and a little over two years ago, it was replaced by the LCI (Life Cycle Impulse), which is Bimmer slang for facelift. The 2er Coupe shouldn’t be confused with the 2 Series Gran Coupe, because it is based on the CLAR (Linie Klein) platform, just like the old 3 Series, 5 Series, 6 Series, X3, X4, Z4, and others, including the M2.
The Gran Coupe on the other hand shares nothing but the 2 Series name with the two-door model, because it is based on the same platform as the F70 1 Series, as well as the 2 Series Active Tourer, the X1, X2, MINI Countryman, and others. All of these rides utilize the front-biased UKL2 construction, whereas the 2er Coupe is a rear-biased machine, just like the larger 3 Series, 4 Series, and so on.
And since we mentioned the M2 two paragraphs above, we should remind you that the second-generation is only three years old, and was joined by an xDrive all-wheel drive variant earlier this year. Launched for the 2027 model year, it is called the M2 M xDrive Coupe, and boasts the same amount of power as its rear-wheel drive sibling.
Photo: Instagram | rotislav_prokop This means 473 horsepower (480 ps/353 kW ) at 6,250 rpm and 443 pound-feet (600 Nm) of torque from 2,700 to 5,620 rpm, which makes it a bit less punchy than the M2 CS . The latter has 523 hp (530 ps/390 kW) and 479 lb-ft (650 Nm) of torque to play with, and can hit 60 mph (97 kph) in just 3.7 seconds. That’s actually one-tenth of a second slower than the M2 M xDrive Coupe, whereas the RWD M2 Coupe will reach 60 mph in 4.1 seconds.
BMW’s M2 CS starts at $98,600 in the United States of America, so it is one pricey cookie. The M2 M xDrive Coupe has an MSRP of $73,600, according to the company’s official local website, whereas the regular M2 Coupe, aka the rear-wheel drive one, kicks off at $69,500. The M240i xDrive Coupe and the M240i Coupe start at $55,600 and $53,600, and have 386 hp (391 ps/288 kW) on tap, taking 4.1 and 4.4 seconds from 0 to 60 mph (97 kph), respectively.
Now, given that the second-gen BMW M2 has been around for three years, we have seen quite a few tuning takes on it. However, one of the latest to have crossed our screens is also on the fake side of things. Why is that, you ask? Because the tuning fairy is actually a rendering fairy in this case, as the pictured project came from @rotislav_prokop on social media.
The CGI artist rearranged the pixels of this machine in order to make it look a lot more appealing, and before inviting you to leave your impression in the comments box at the bottom of the story, we should delve into some of the things that make this car stand out. These include the extremely wide front fenders and rear three-quarter panels, which make it look like it belongs at the racetrack and not on public roads.
Photo: Instagram | rotislav_prokop Up front, it has been virtually altered with a modified bumper, as well as a fat apron, and there are side skirt extensions on deck, too, as well as a modified rear bumper that is significantly wider than before, a new diffuser with a motorsport-like extra brake light in the middle, and a ducktail spoiler.

The alloys, with their wide lips and visible rivets, mix a silver and black finish, and the suspension has also been tuned.
According to the rendering artist behind these digital illustrations, this BMW M2 is said to have a “ more elegant attitude, ” and “ the goal ” was to make it “ wider, more distinctive, and more sophisticated, while keeping the character that makes the M2 so special. ” I definitely dig the makeover, and I think that this thing would have been a lot cooler if it featured a racing-inspired livery. Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) wants to bring back the federal EV tax credit and double it. His new bill, the “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” (H.R. 10881), would offer up to $15,000 on a new electric vehicle and $8,000 on a used one, and it would make both credits permanent.
The problem is that the bill has virtually no chance of becoming law anytime soon. And if EV shoppers start holding out for it, it could end up hurting the market it’s trying to help.
What’s in the bill
Landsman introduced H.R. 10881 on October 22. It was referred to three House committees (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources), and as of today, it doesn’t have a single cosponsor.
The big change is to the new clean vehicle credit, Section 30D of the tax code. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, the $7,500 credit came in two $3,750 halves: one for meeting critical mineral sourcing requirements and one for battery components. Landsman’s bill doubles each half to $7,500, for a maximum of $15,000.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
It also deletes the termination dates. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed the new and used EV credits for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and the home charger credit after June 30, 2026. Striking those dates would revive all three credits with no expiration.
Here are the other changes:
The used EV credit goes from $4,000 or 30% of the sale price (whichever is lower) to $8,000 or 60%.
The charging equipment credit goes from 30% to 50% of the cost.
The income caps on the new EV credit drop by 25%: $225,000 for joint filers (from $300,000), $169,000 for heads of household (from $225,000), and $112,500 for single filers (from $150,000).
It’s once per taxpayer. Anyone who was allowed the 30D credit in any previous tax year gets $0. As written, that isn’t limited to credits claimed after the bill passes, so everyone who used the credit between 2023 and 2025 would be shut out.
The bill doesn’t touch the rest of 30D. North American final assembly, the $55,000 MSRP cap on cars and $80,000 cap on SUVs, pickups, and vans, and the foreign entity of concern rules all stay. So the full $15,000 would only go to EVs that clear both sourcing tests, which has always been a short list.
The rest of the bill is reports. Commerce would deliver a “Vehicle Choice Report” on vehicle variety and ownership costs, and the Department of Energy would file five years of critical minerals reports.
The most interesting part is a DOE study of “gasoline super-users,” defined as the top 10% of light-duty vehicle owners by gas consumption. The study would map the regions where they’re concentrated and their 100 most-used routes, then track charger availability along those routes every year for five years. Coltura, which backs the bill, says the highest-mileage drivers spend over 10% of household income on fuel.
No realistic path to becoming law
Republicans control both the House and the Senate, and they’re the ones who just repealed these credits. President Trump signed that repeal.
Even if Democrats flip the House and Senate in next week’s midterms, a bill restoring EV credits would still need to get through a veto. So realistically, nothing like this happens before 2029.
It’s also a rerun. Landsman introduced the exact same “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” as H.R. 10046 on October 25, 2024, 11 days before that year’s election. It got zero cosponsors and died in committee. This version landed 12 days before the November 3 midterms.
The risk: buyers waiting for a credit that isn’t coming
This is where the bill can do real damage. EV buyers are extremely sensitive to tax credit timing, and the last year proved it.
When the credit was about to disappear, buyers rushed in, and Q3 2025 became the best quarter ever for US EV sales, with market share topping 10% for the first time. Then the floor dropped out. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 sales fell 63% the month after the credit ended.
The market is only now crawling back. According to Cox Automotive , US EV sales hit 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% from Q2 but still down 39.5% year-over-year, at a 6.4% share of new vehicle sales. Tesla’s Model Y and Model 3 still dominate, but Toyota, Rivian, and Hyundai are growing again .
That recovery is fragile. A headline promising “$15,000 off your next EV” is exactly what makes a shopper on the fence decide to wait a year or two.
And waiting gets you nothing. The new credits would only apply to vehicles placed in service after the bill is enacted, so there’s no retroactive payout for buying now. If you already claimed the credit once, you’d get $0 anyway.
Meanwhile, the deals on the lot are real. Automakers have been cutting prices to make up for the lost credit, like Hyundai, which cut the 2026 Ioniq 5 by nearly $10,000 on some trims.
Electrek’s Take
At Electrek, our position has always been clear: we think EVs are a net positive and ICE vehicles have unpriced externalities. Therefore, we will take whatever we can get to encourage EV sales, but our preferred approach would be a carbon tax on ICE vehicles.
We’ve been clear that policy shapes this market. Killing the $7,500 credit is the main reason US EV sales collapsed. Consumers didn’t suddenly decide they hate EVs. So we’re all for bringing incentives back.
But this bill is messaging. It has zero cosponsors and no CBO score, and it dropped two weeks before an election, just like the identical version two years ago.

To be fair, some of it is smart. The lower income caps and the once-per-taxpayer limit go after the most common criticism of the old credit, that it subsidized wealthy households buying their second or third EV. And the “super-user” study is the best idea in the bill. Getting a high-mileage driver out of a gas pickup does far more for fuel costs and emissions than putting a low-mileage commuter in their second Tesla. If Democrats want to rebuild EV policy in 2029, that’s where they should start.
The problem is that people will hear the headline number. If you need a car now and an EV fits your life, buy it now and take the deals that are on the table. Don’t plan your purchase around a bill that has no path to passing for at least two years.
Will Democrats come back with a real, cosponsored EV plan before 2028? I don’t know, but I suspect that the US will continue to fall behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption.
